inline.s: Gathering karma makes consciousness; the un-gathering makes wisdom,
Contemplating all dharmas, one penetrates to nothing at all.
Attaining the power of freedom, this is then called wisdom,
Bound to sense-objects is the mind; when the awareness of thinking arises, that is wisdom.
From the nothing-at-all and the supreme, wisdom is thereby born,
The mind, intention, and consciousness, far from thinking and ideation.
Attaining the Dharma of no-thought, the Buddha’s child is no śrāvaka,
The still, supreme, advancing patience is the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom.
Born in the good supreme meaning, all that is practiced is left far behind,
I have three kinds of wisdom, which the noble unfold as the real.
Through that ideation and thinking, all natures are grasped,
the two vehicles are not in accord with it, and wisdom is free of all possessions.
Clinging to self-nature arises in the śrāvakas,
transcending all the measures of mind, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.

Moreover, Mahāmati! Non-Buddhists set forth nine theories of transformation. From their views of transformation arise, namely: transformation of shape, transformation of characteristic, transformation of cause, transformation of accomplishment, transformation of view, transformation of nature, transformation of the clear discrimination of causes, transformation of the clear discrimination of actions, and transformation of things. Mahāmati! These are called the nine views of transformation. All non-Buddhists, on account of these, develop the theories of arising, non-arising, and transformation. What is transformation of shape? It is the seeing of a change in shape. For example, when gold is made into various vessels, there appear various shapes, yet the nature of gold does not change. So too with all transformations of nature. Or, some non-Buddhists entertain such an imagination, even the imagination of the transformation of things — yet these are neither real nor different, being mere delusion. Thus all transformations of nature should be known as the ripening of milk, curd, wine, and fruits. In the non-Buddhists’ imagination of transformation, there is in truth no transformation; whether existence or non-existence, it is presented by one’s own mind, and external nature is not real. Mahāmati! Such foolish common beings are born of their own delusive habitual practices. Mahāmati! There is no dharma that arises or perishes, just as when one sees the colors born in an illusion or a dream.”
Transformation of shape, time, and change — the four great elements and the faculties,
arise progressively in the intermediate state; such delusion is not clear wisdom.
The supremely wise one, in dependent arising, is not like those delusions,
yet worldly dependent arising is like a gandharva city.”

At that time the bodhisattva Mahāmati again said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, may the Blessed One be pleased to explain the meaning of the connectedness of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation. If I and the bodhisattvas can well discriminate the characteristics of the connectedness and non-connectedness of all dharmas, then we shall skillfully understand the skillful means of all connectedness, and not fall into clinging to connectedness as it is spoken of. Skilled in the characteristics of the connectedness and non-connectedness of all dharmas, and free of the delusive awareness of words and letters, we shall wander through all Buddha-lands, amid countless assemblies, with the seal of the power of freedom, psychic powers, and dhāraṇī, with various transformations and shining light. With awareness and wisdom we shall well enter the ten inexhaustible sentences, without expedient practices. Like the sun, moon, jewel, and the four great elements, in all the grounds we shall be free of the characteristics of our own delusive views, and see all dharmas as like illusions or dreams. Entering the Buddha’s ground-body, in all the realms of sentient beings we shall teach the Dharma for each as is fitting and guide them, causing them all to abide [in the view that] all dharmas are like illusions or dreams — free of the categories of existence and non-existence and of the delusions of arising and perishing, [seeing] the meanings beyond words — and their own bodies will become ever more excellent.’
The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Well said, well said! Listen carefully, listen carefully! Think of it well, and I will speak to you.’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘The immeasurable all dharmas, as they are spoken of, are clung to as connected. Namely: clinging to characteristics as connected; clinging to conditions as connected; clinging to nature and non-nature as connected; the delusion of arising and non-arising clung to as connected; the delusion of ceasing and non-ceasing clung to as connected; the delusion of vehicle and non-vehicle clung to as connected; the delusion of conditioned and unconditioned clung to as connected; the delusion of the self-characteristics of each ground clung to as connected; the uninterrupted delusion of one’s own delusions clung to as connected; the categories of existence and non-existence to which non-Buddhists cling, relying on delusion, as connected; and the delusion of the three vehicles and the one vehicle as continuous, clung to as connected. Moreover, Mahāmati! These and other foolish common beings have their own delusive connectedness. Because of this connectedness, the delusions of the foolish are like a silkworm making a cocoon; with the threads of delusion they bind themselves and bind others, clinging to the connected characteristics of existence and non-existence. Moreover, Mahāmati! In this, there is actually neither the characteristic of connectedness nor of non-connectedness. Because one sees all dharmas as still, delusive thinking does not arise. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees all dharmas as still. Moreover, Mahāmati! Realizing that external nature is not real, the characteristics presented by one’s own mind are nothing at all. In accordance with contemplating the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind, in existence and non-existence all natures are without characteristics; because it sees connectedness as still, in all dharmas there is neither the characteristic of connectedness nor of non-connectedness. Moreover, Mahāmati! In this there is neither binding nor release. Others, falling into not truly realizing [this], maintain there is binding and release. Why? Because with regard to all dharmas there is neither existence nor non-existence, and no sentient being is obtainable.’

Moreover, Mahāmati! Fools have three [kinds of] connectedness, namely: greed, anger, and delusion, and the craving for the future, together with the delight of clinging to existence. Because of this connectedness, there is the connectedness of [the] destinies; those who are connected continue through the five destinies. Mahāmati! For one in whom connectedness is cut off, there is neither the characteristic of connectedness nor of non-connectedness. Moreover, Mahāmati! Through the three-fold conjunction of conditions, one makes expedient clinging, and the connectedness of consciousness arises uninterruptedly. Through expedient clinging, there is connectedness. When, through the three-fold conjunction of conditions, consciousness is cut off, one sees the three liberations, and all connectedness does not arise.”
Unreal delusion is declared to be the characteristic of connectedness,
If one knows that reality, the net of connectedness is cut.
Being without knowledge of all natures, one grasps according to words,
like that silkworm, weaving a net and binding itself,
fools are bound by delusion, not observing connectedness.”

Mahāmati again said to the Buddha: ‘As the Blessed One has said, by means of these and those delusions one imagines these and those natures; there is no such self-nature in them, only the self-nature of delusion itself.’

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, if it is only the self-nature of delusion, and [in reality] there is no nature or self-nature for it to be correlated with, does the Blessed One not fall into the fault of [saying that] both defilement and purity are without nature, since the self-nature of the delusion of all dharmas is no-nature?’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘So it is, so it is! As you have said. Mahāmati! It is not as fools, whose delusions about self-nature are real. This self-nature of delusion does not truly have a characteristic of self-nature. Mahāmati! Just as the noble one’s wisdom has a self-nature — by the noble one’s knowledge, the noble one’s vision, the noble one’s eye of wisdom — so one knows that self-nature.’

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘If, like the noble one, with the noble one’s knowledge, the noble one’s vision, the noble one’s eye of wisdom — not the divine eye, not the fleshly eye — one knows self-nature thus, and not as fools’ delusion, then, O Blessed One, how is it that fools, being apart from this delusion, are unaware of the matter of the noble nature? O Blessed One, they are neither inverted nor not inverted. Why? Because they are not aware of the self-nature of the noble matter, and therefore do not see the characteristic that is free of existence and non-existence. O Blessed One, the noble one also does not see thus; such a delusion does not take the characteristics of self as its realm. O Blessed One, the self-nature of this delusion appears thus; it is not spoken of as having a cause or as having no cause, because it falls into the view of the characteristics of nature. Different realms, unlike those of such ones — thus the faults are endless. O Blessed One, [this is] because they are not aware of the characteristics of self-nature. O Blessed One, it is also not even a self-nature of delusion that is the cause of the characteristic of self-nature. How do they take delusion as non-delusion, and truly know delusion? O Blessed One, delusion is different, and the characteristic of self-nature is different. O Blessed One, with a dissimilar cause, one imagines the self-nature of delusion. How do they, variously, not imagine, while fools do not truly know, and yet, for the sake of sentient beings’ separation from delusion, say that such characteristics of delusion are not truly real? O Blessed One, why does the Blessed One restrain sentient beings from clinging to the self-nature of things seen as existing and non-existing, and yet fall into the view of existence [through] clinging to the realm where the noble one’s wisdom moves, saying that dharmas, being empty, are without nature, and yet speak of the self-nature of the noble wisdom’s matter?’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘It is not that I say dharmas, being empty, are without nature, nor that I fall into the view of existence when I speak of the matter of the self-nature of the noble wisdom; rather, it is to cause sentient beings to be free of the phrase [that makes them] afraid. From beginningless time sentient beings have clung to the characteristics of self-nature, and clinging to the characteristics in their view of the self-nature of the noble wisdom’s matter, I speak of the emptiness of dharmas. Mahāmati! I do not speak of the characteristic of self-nature. Mahāmati! But I abide in the Dharma of emptiness that I myself have attained, free of the characteristics of delusion and confusion, free of the views of nature and non-nature presented by my own mind. Attaining the three liberations, I am sealed with the seal of reality. Abiding in the self-realized contemplation of self-nature through conditions, I am free of the characteristics of the views of existence and non-existence with respect to things. Moreover, Mahāmati! Regarding [the claim that] “all dharmas do not arise,” a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not set up such a tenet. Why? Because [in] that tenet all natures have no nature, and because of the characteristic of arising by cause [involved] in it. If one says “all dharmas do not arise,” that tenet is then refuted. That tenet — “all dharmas do not arise” — is refuted because the tenet depends [on something] to arise. Further, that tenet of non-arising enters into all dharmas, and because there is the non-arising of the un-refuted characteristic. One who sets up the tenet “all dharmas do not arise” — his teaching is refuted. Mahāmati! The tenet of “neither existence nor non-existence and no arising” enters into all natures; the characteristics of existence and non-existence are not obtainable. Mahāmati! If that tenet of non-arising is set up because all natures do not arise, then that tenet is refuted. Because the nature and non-nature of existence do not arise, one should not set up the tenet. Because of the many faults of the five-membered treatise, because of the different characteristics of successive causes, and because it is [itself] made, one should not set up the tenet “all dharmas do not arise”; likewise, one should not set up “all dharmas are empty,” nor “all dharmas have no self-nature.” Mahāmati! Yet a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when he says all dharmas are like illusions or dreams — which is because of the characteristics of appearing and not appearing, and because of the faults of perception and awareness — should speak of the nature of all dharmas as like illusions or dreams, except only to free fools from the phrase [that makes them] afraid. Mahāmati! Fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to be afraid, [lest] they turn away from the Mahāyāna.’
At that time the Blessed One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again, spoke in verse:
Without self-nature and without speech, without things and without connectedness,
the fools’ delusion is like the foul notion of a corpse.
“All dharmas do not arise” is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists,
ultimately nothing is born; nature is accomplished by conditions.
“All dharmas do not arise” — the wise one forms no such thought,
because that tenet [itself] arises by cause, the awakened one removes it entirely.
As when one with dim eyes looks and falsely sees the mark of a falling hair,
so it is with clinging to nature; such are the fools’ wrong delusions.
What is set up in the three realms has no self-nature of things,
setting up the self-nature of things, thinking gives rise to delusion.
Characteristics and things are set up in words and teachings, the mind confused and violently distraught,
but the Buddha’s children are able to transcend and be far from all delusions.
What is not water is received as water; this arises from craving-thirst,
the foolish are thus deluded, but the noble one’s vision is not so.
The noble one sees purity; the three liberations and samādhis arise,
far from birth and death, wandering without fear.
Practicing with nothing at all, and also neither nature nor non-nature,
nature and non-nature are equal, and from this the noble fruit is born.
How are nature and non-nature [equal]? What is equality?
It is that the mind, not knowing, is tossed about within and without,
but if one can destroy that, the mind then sees equally.”

At that time the bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, as the Blessed One has said, regarding the matter of clinging, wisdom does not attain [it]; it is a measure set up and an established designation. What is grasped is not a nature, and the grasping too is not a nature. Because there is no grasping, wisdom does not arise; there is only a set-up name. How is this, O Blessed One? Is it because [wisdom] does not realize the self-characteristics and common characteristics [of natures] as being different or not different, that wisdom does not attain? Or is it because the self-characteristics and common characteristics and the self-nature characteristics of various natures are hidden, that wisdom does not attain? Or is it because of the hindrance of mountains, rocks, and cliffs, of earth, water, fire, and wind, that wisdom does not attain? Or is it because of what is extremely far and extremely near, that wisdom does not attain? Or is it because of the old, the young, the blind, and the confused, with incomplete faculties, that wisdom does not attain? O Blessed One, if, not realizing the difference and non-difference of self-characteristics and common characteristics, wisdom does not attain, then one should not call it wisdom; one should call it non-wisdom, because the matter [of attainment] is not obtainable. And if, because the self-characteristics and common characteristics and the self-nature characteristics of various natures are hidden, wisdom does not attain, that too is non-wisdom, not wisdom. O Blessed One, because there is the object-realm (ālambana), wisdom arises; it is not that, without nature, one meets the object-realm, [such a one’s wisdom] being called wisdom. If, because of mountains, rocks, cliffs, earth, water, fire, wind, the extremely far and the extremely near, the old, the young, the blind, and the confused, with incomplete faculties, wisdom does not attain, then this too is not wisdom; it should be non-wisdom, because the matter [of attainment] is not obtainable.’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Not so. Non-wisdom should be [called] wisdom; it is not that it is not wisdom. It is not by my concealing [realization] and speaking of the matter of clinging, [as if] wisdom does not attain, [that] it is a measure set up and an established designation. Awakening to the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind, [seeing that] existence, non-existence, and external nature are not real, [there is] wisdom, yet the matter is not attained. Because it is not attained, wisdom does not arise with regard to the object-realm. In accord with the three liberations, wisdom too is not attained. It is not that, for one who is not deluded, from beginningless time there is the false habitual knowledge of nature and non-nature, [and so] one thus knows [in a way] that is knowing that which they do not know. Therefore, with regard to the places of external things, one makes nature into non-nature, and delusion is uninterrupted. By the establishment of the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind, one speaks of the characteristics of self and mine, grasping and clinging. Not awakening to the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind, one gives rise to delusion with regard to wisdom’s object-realm. Because of delusion, external nature is [seen as] not real, and, contemplating, one does not attain, and one relies on the nihilistic view.’
There are matters of clinging that wisdom does not observe,
this is non-wisdom, not wisdom, as one who is deluded says.
With regard to characteristics and natures that are not different, wisdom does not observe,
obstruction and nearness and farness — these are called wrong wisdom.
The old, the young, the faculties dark, and wisdom not arising,
though there is truly an object-realm — this too is called wrong wisdom.

Moreover, Mahāmati! Foolish common beings, from beginningless time turned about by false, evil, wrong delusions, when thus turned about, do not well understand self-tenet-penetration and word-penetration. Because they cling to the external characteristics presented by their own mind, they cling to expedient speech, and do not well discriminate the pure penetrative characteristics of the four phrases of their own teaching.”

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘Truly as the Blessed One teaches. May the Blessed One be pleased to explain to me word-penetration and tenet-penetration. Then I and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas, being skilled in these two penetrations, [will see] that the fools, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the future cannot find their fault.’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘The Tathāgatas of the three times have two kinds of Dharma-penetration, namely: word-penetration and self-tenet-penetration. Word-penetration is: in accordance with the responding minds of sentient beings, to speak for them various complete sūtras — this is called word-penetration. Self-tenet-penetration is: the practitioner, free of the various delusions presented by his own mind — that is, not falling into the categories of one and different, both and neither — transcending all mind, intention, and consciousness, [abiding in] the self-realized noble realm, free of the views of characteristics constituted by causes, which all the non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas who fall into the two extremes are unable to know. I call this the self-tenet-penetration Dharma. Mahāmati! These are the characteristics of self-tenet-penetration and word-penetration. You and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas should study them.’
I have two kinds of penetration: tenet-penetration and word-speech,
the speaker teaches the childlike; the tenet is for the practitioner.”

At that time the bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, as the Blessed One once said: “The various disputations of worldly treatises — be careful not to draw near to them or study them. If one draws near to them, one takes up greed and does not take up the Dharma.” Why, O Blessed One, did the Blessed One speak thus?’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘The words and disputations of worldly treatises, with their various phrases, causes, and similes, learned and adorned, attract and deceive foolish common beings. They do not enter the true self-penetration, do not realize all dharmas, and, deluded and inverted, fall into the two extremes. The common and foolish, deluded and confused, destroy themselves; continued in the various destinies, they do not attain liberation; they cannot awaken to the immediate measure presented by their own mind, and are not free of external nature and self-nature, clinging in delusion. Therefore the various disputations of worldly treatises do not transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering; they deceive and confuse. Mahāmati! Śakra, lord of the devas, widely expounded the many treatises and himself composed the treatise on sound. That worldly philosopher had a disciple who, bearing the form of a dragon, went to the palace of the devas, established a philosophical tenet, and pledged to break Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel: “If my [tenet] should lose, I will cut off my heads one by one to atone for my defeat.” Having thus pledged, he used Śakra’s own reasoning to defeat Śakra. Śakra, falling into defeat, broke his own wheel and returned to the world. Thus, Mahāmati! worldly treatises, by the adornment of similes — even animals — can, with various phrases, delude those devas and asuras who cling to the views of arising and perishing, and how much more human beings. Therefore, Mahāmati! worldly treatises should be left far behind, because they are the cause that brings about suffering; be careful not to draw near to them or study them. Mahāmati! The worldly philosophers speak only of the realm of the body’s experience. Mahāmati! Those worldly philosophers number in the hundreds and thousands, yet in later times, in the last fifty years, they will destroy the compilation [of the Dharma]. Because their wrong views and views of causes flourish, evil disciples will receive [their teaching]. Thus, Mahāmati! The worldly treatises destroy the compilation, with various phrases, causes, and similes, adorned, speaking of the affairs of the non-Buddhists, clinging to their own causes and conditions, and having no self-penetration. Mahāmati! Those non-Buddhists, with the treatises [lacking] self-penetration, in their other worldly treatises widely expound countless hundreds of thousands of matters, and, with no self-penetration, do not themselves know the foolishness of [their] worldly treatises.’

At that time Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, if the worldly treatises of the non-Buddhists, with their various phrases, causes, and similes, adorned, have no self-penetration and cling to their own matters, then does the Blessed One also speak worldly treatises, for the various assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras who come from different regions, widely expounding countless phrases — is this too not self-penetration? Does it also fall into the number of the wisdom and speech of all the non-Buddhists?’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘I do not speak worldly treatises, nor have I any coming or going; I speak only of not coming and not going. Mahāmati! What comes is the arising of gathering in assemblies; what goes is scattering and destruction. What neither comes nor goes is non-arising and non-ceasing. What I speak does not fall into the number of the delusions of worldly treatises. Why? Because for one who does not reckon [in them], external nature is not real, [this being] the place presented by one’s own mind — the delusions of the two extremes cannot turn him. The characteristics and sense-objects are not real; awakening to what one’s own mind presents, then, since it is [all] presented by one’s own mind, delusion does not arise. What is free of delusion is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; entering the three gates of liberation, this is called liberation. Mahāmati! I recall once, dwelling in a certain place, there came to me a worldly-philosopher brahmin. Without waiting for a moment of leisure, he asked me: “Gotama! Is everything made?” I then replied: “Brahmin! That everything is made is the first worldly treatise.” He asked again: “Is everything not made?” I replied: “That everything is not made is the second worldly treatise.” He asked again: “Is everything eternal? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything not born?” I replied: “That is six worldly treatises.” Mahāmati! He asked me again: “Is everything one? Is everything different? Is everything both? Is everything neither? Does everything arise as various kinds of rebirth?” I replied: “That is eleven worldly treatises.” Mahāmati! He asked again: “Is everything indeterminate? Is everything determinate? Is there a self? Is there no self? Is there this world? Is there no this world? Is there another world? Is there no other world? Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Is everything momentary? Is everything not momentary? Is there space? Is there non-analytic cessation? Is there nirvāṇa? Gotama! Is [it] made? Is [it] not made? Is there an intermediate state? Is there no intermediate state?” Mahāmati! I replied: “Brahmin! All such assertions are worldly treatises. It is not what I speak; they are your worldly treatises. I speak only of the various evils of the false, delusive habitual tendencies, which from beginningless time are the causes of the three realms [of existence] — [beings] cannot awaken to the immediate measure presented by their own mind and so give rise to delusion, clinging to external nature. As in the non-Buddhists’ Dharma, [by] my faculties and meanings, the wisdom of the three-fold conjunction arises. Not so am I, Brahmin! I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no cause. I speak only of the nature of the grasped and the grasping in delusion, and the dependent arising set up [therein], which neither you, nor others who fall into the continuation of grasping self, can awaken to.” Mahāmati! Nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not three [separate] natures; only the number is three.’

Moreover, Mahāmati! Then the worldly-philosopher brahmin again asked me: “Is there threefold existence because of the karmic cause of delusion and craving? Or is it without cause?” I replied: “These two are also merely worldly treatises.” He asked again: “Do all natures enter into these self-characteristics and common characteristics?” I replied: “This too is a worldly treatise. Brahmin! Even the flowing of the mind falsely reckoning external sense-dusts — all of it is a worldly treatise.”

Moreover, Mahāmati! Then the worldly-philosopher brahmin again asked me: “Is there something that is not a worldly treatise? I am the [chief] tenet of all the non-Buddhists, speaking various phrases, causes, and similes, adorned.” I replied: “Brahmin! There is something that is not yours: it is non-doing, non-tenet, non-speech, and non-non-speech of various phrases, and not without causes and similes, adorned.” The brahmin said: “What is the non-worldly-treatise, the non-non-tenet, the non-non-speech?” I replied: “Brahmin! There is a non-worldly-treatise, which you non-Buddhists are unable to know, because you cling falsely and delusively to unreal external nature. Namely: when delusion does not arise, and one awakens to the existence and non-existence and the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind — delusion does not arise, one does not receive external sense-dusts, and delusion is forever stilled. This is called non-worldly-treatise. This is my Dharma; it is not yours. Brahmin! In brief, that consciousness, whether coming or going, whether dying or being born, whether blissful or painful, whether immersed or seen, whether touched or clung to, with its various characteristics — whether in harmonious continuation, whether in feeling, whether in the clinging of causes — Brahmin! All such as these are your worldly treatises, not mine.” Mahāmati! The worldly-philosopher brahmin, having asked thus and been answered thus, fell silent, and without taking leave went away. Pondering in his own penetration place, he thought: “The Śākyan renunciant, going beyond [all] penetration, speaks of non-arising, non-characteristic, and non-cause, awakening to what one’s own delusion presents, and delusion does not arise.” Mahāmati! This is what you asked me before: “Why did [the Blessed One] speak of drawing near to the various disputations of worldly treatises, taking up greed and not taking up the Dharma?”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, what is the meaning of the phrases “taking up greed” and “taking up the Dharma”?’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Well said, well said! You are able, for the sake of the sentient beings of the future, to think of and inquire into such a meaning of phrases. Listen carefully, listen carefully! Think of it well, and I will speak to you.’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘What is called greed — whether taking, or rejecting, or touching, or tasting, bound to external sense-dusts, falling into the views of the two extremes — again gives rise to the aggregate of suffering: birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering. Such afflictions all arise from craving; this is because one draws near to worldly treatises and to the worldly philosophers. I and the Buddhas call this greed. This is called taking up greed and not taking up the Dharma. Mahāmati! What is to take up the Dharma? It is to well awaken to the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind, to see the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of dharmas, and to have delusion not arise. Well knowing the grounds, upper and lower
(the “Dan” edition)

, free of mind, intention, and consciousness, receiving the consecration of the wisdom of all the Buddhas, fully taking up the ten inexhaustible sentences, and in all dharmas being free and spontaneous without [further] unfolding — this is called the Dharma. Namely, not falling into any view, any falsehood, any delusion, any nature, or any of the two extremes. Mahāmati! There are many foolish non-Buddhists who fall into the two extremes, whether eternalism or nihilism; they are not wise. Receiving the doctrine of no-cause, they give rise to the eternalist view; [holding] that external causes destroy causes and conditions, [and] nature is no-nature, they give rise to the nihilist view. Mahāmati! Because I do not see arising, abiding, and ceasing, I call it the Dharma. Mahāmati! This is greed and the Dharma. You and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas should study them.’
All worldly treatises are the false speech of non-Buddhists,
they falsely see the maker and the made, and they have no self-tenet.
Only I have one self-tenet, free of the maker and the made,
which I speak for my disciples, [teaching] to be far from all worldly treatises.
The measure of mind is invisible; one does not observe the two minds,
the grasped and the grasping are not real, and both eternalism and nihilism are left behind,
even the flowing of mind is then a worldly treatise.
For one whose delusion does not turn, that one sees his own mind;
what comes is called the arising of a thing; what goes is the thing’s not appearing.
Clearly knowing coming and going, delusion arises no more,
existence, eternal and impermanent, the made and the unmade,
this world, other worlds, and so on — all are [but] the penetration of worldly treatises.”

At that time the bodhisattva Mahāmati again said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, what is that Dharma which is called nirvāṇa? And the various non-Buddhists each give rise to their own delusions [about it].’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Listen carefully, listen carefully! Think of it well, and I will speak to you. As for the delusions of the various non-Buddhists about nirvāṇa, it is not that their delusions accord with nirvāṇa.’

The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Some non-Buddhists, [holding] that the aggregates, realms, and sense-fields cease, [that there is] freedom from sense-objects, seeing dharmas as impermanent, [that] the categories of mind and mental factors do not arise, not mindful of the realms of the past, future, and present, [and that] the aggregates of feeling are exhausted — as when a lamp is extinguished, as when a seed is broken, delusion no longer arises. Such ones, in regard to this, form the idea of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati! It is not that what is seen being broken is called nirvāṇa. Mahāmati! Some, [holding] the going from one region to another, call this liberation, [when] the ideation of realms is extinguished, like the wind ceasing. Or again, [holding] that what is perceived and the perception of it are broken, they call this liberation. Or seeing the eternal and the impermanent, they form the idea of liberation. Or seeing the ideation of various characteristics that brings about the cause of suffering, and having pondered this, not well awakening to the immediate measure presented by their own mind, frightened of characteristics, they see the signless, and deeply loving it, they form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some, realizing the inner and outer dharmas, their self-characteristics and common characteristics, past, future, and present, as having an unbroken nature, form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some hold that self, person, sentient being, and life, [and] all dharmas, are broken — [and] form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some, with the evil fire of non-Buddhist [views] burning wisdom, see self-nature and a purusha (primordial person); these two have an interval, and what the purusha produces is called self-nature. Like the comparison with the primordial dark, then the guṇa transformation — the guṇa being the maker — [thus] they form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some say that merit and non-merit are exhausted; or some say that the afflictions are exhausted; or some say [it is] wisdom. Or some see Īśvara as the true maker of birth and death — [and] form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some hold that there is successive mutual arising, and that birth and death have no other cause — this very [notion] is clinging to a cause, and those foolish ones cannot awaken to it. Not knowing, they form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some non-Buddhists say that they have attained the true path — [and] form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some see the merits and the harmonious efflorescence that merits produce, [in terms of] one and different, both and neither — [and] form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some see the peacock’s patterns produced by self-nature, the various jewels, and the nature of thorns — having seen [these], they form the idea of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati! Or some realize the twenty-five truths, or [hold that] a king, guarding the state, receives the six-merit treatise — [and] form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or some see time as the maker, the seasons and the world; those who thus realize form the idea of nirvāṇa. Or they speak of nature, or of non-nature, or of knowing nature and non-nature, or they see a difference between awareness and nirvāṇa — [and] form the idea of nirvāṇa. Such are the various delusions that non-Buddhists speak of, which do not accomplish what should be accomplished, and are rejected by the wise. Mahāmati! All of these, entirely falling into the two extremes, form the idea of nirvāṇa. These delusions of the non-Buddhists about nirvāṇa — in them there is neither arising nor ceasing. Mahāmati! Each and every non-Buddhist nirvāṇa, they maintain in their own treatises; observing with wisdom, nothing at all is established. Like their delusion, the mind and intention come and go, drifting and flowing; of all of them, there is no one who attains nirvāṇa. Mahāmati! As I speak of nirvāṇa: it is to well awaken to the immediate measure presented by one’s own mind

There are four measures: first, immediate seeing; second, inference; third, simile; fourth, the tradition handed down from the ancient sages. With these four measures, the non-Buddhists all fail [to establish their case].

— not clinging to external nature, free of the four phrases, seeing the place of reality, not following the two extremes of the delusions presented by one’s own mind, [so that] the grasped and the grasping are not obtainable. All measures see nothing that is accomplished; being foolish about reality, one should not receive [such measures]. Having abandoned them, one attains the self-realized noble Dharma. Knowing the two selflessnesses, free of the two afflictions, purely clearing the two hindrances, forever free of the two deaths, [and] in the highest grounds [up to] the Tathāgata ground, in the deep samādhis like reflections and illusions, free of mind, intention, and consciousness — this is called nirvāṇa. Mahāmati! You and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas should study this and swiftly be far from all the views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists.’
The non-Buddhists’ views of nirvāṇa, each giving rise to its own delusion,
arise from thought and mind; they have no means of liberation.
Fools, bound to the bound, are far from the good means,
and from the non-Buddhists’ idea of liberation, liberation never arises.
The many wisdoms have various aims; what the non-Buddhists see is [but] common,
and all of them have no liberation, because of foolish delusion.
All foolish non-Buddhists falsely see the maker and the made,
and the categories of existence and non-existence in their treatises; of them all, none has liberation.
Common fools delight in delusion and do not hear the real wisdom,
words are the root of the three sufferings; the real is the cause that quenches suffering.
As with an image in a mirror, though it appears yet is not real,
in the mirror of the delusive mind, fools see a duality.
Not knowing mind and its conditions, one gives rise to the delusion of duality,
understanding mind and its objects, delusion does not arise.
For the mind is the manifold, far from the characteristic and the characterized,
things appear yet do not appear, like those fools’ delusions.
The three realms are only delusion; external objects are all non-existent,
delusion manifests in various ways, which the common and foolish cannot understand.
Sūtra after sūtra speaks of delusion, [which] never goes beyond names,
and if one leaves speech, there is nothing [that can be] said.”

The Heart of All the Buddha’s Words, Chapter Four

At that time the bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, may the Blessed One be pleased to speak of the truly and fully enlightened Buddha. Then I and the other bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas will be skilled in the Tathāgata’s self-nature, awakening self and awakening others.’
The Buddha told Mahāmati: ‘Ask as you wish, and I will speak to you in accordance with your question.’

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Worthy of Offerings, the Fully Enlightened One — is he the maker? Or the not-maker? Is he the action? Or the cause? Is he the characteristic? Or the characterized? Is he the speaker? Or the spoken? Is he the awakener? Or the awakened? Are such phrases as these different or not different?’
